newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Le Pen attacks Chirac, Europe, immigrants.
newsitem.headline: France's Le Pen attacks Chirac, Europe, immigrants.

text.p: French far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen and his National Front launched their drive for a toehold in parliament on Thursday with a vitriolic attack on European union, immigrants and conservative President Jacques Chirac.

Before some 9,000 cheering supporters, Le Pen accused Chirac and the centre-right government of ignoring immigration and high unemployment while seeking to jettison France's national identity, and he urged voters to "throw them out" of office.

"You (Chirac) have always betrayed your friends, your ideas, your campaign promises, and today you are asking for a blank cheque to betray France by submerging it in the Europe of Maastricht," Le Pen said ahead of the May-June parliamentary election.

His traditional May Day festival, honouring French mediaeval hero Joan of Arc who drove the English out of France, was broadened this year to carry Front hopes of winning seats in the National Assembly, where it currently has none.

Before Le Pen's speech, Front backers marched in bright sunshine past a gilded statue of Joan of Arc facing the Tuileries gardens and on to the Opera House while across the city leftist trade unions staged their own march.
"Marianne (symbol of the republic), the France I love is without Le Pen," read many banners carried by anti-racism organisations at the union rally.
"It's true that this year the fight against racism, against hatred...takes on a much bigger dimension given the National Front's objectives," Louis Viannet of the Communist CGT union told reporters.

The Front, which wants to ship immigrants home and give a constitutional preference to "native-born French" in jobs, education and social benefits, has set a goal of 20 seats in the elections, enough to form a parliamentary group.
Pollsters predicted it could win at most a few seats, although voter surveys show it gathering rather more than the 15 percent Le Pen won in his 1995 presidential campaign.

Even if the Front fails to win seats, it could play a key role in an estimated 200 or more of France's 577 constituencies by splitting the vote of centre-right candidates. In a worst-case scenario for the centre-right, the Front could shove the left into power.

Le Pen, who announced on the eve of the parade that he would not himself run in the election, barely mentioned the left in his speech, saying the Front's priority was to "zap" the government even if it meant a victory for the left.
"What is being hidden from you is that France is in danger of disappearing...before the end of the century," Le Pen said.
"Chirac is asking you today to give you his consent, to be an accomplice to this national suicide...and it is for this reason that you are going to vote massively for the National Front," he said.
"We must re-establish national sovereignty by renegotiating our agreements on Europe and abandoning the euro," he said.
Two years ago, Le Pen's May 1 celebration was marred when skinheads threw a man of North African origin into the Seine river, where he drowned.
Most in the parade were well-dressed, sporting suits and ties or dresses. But a number of skinheads in leather and heavy boots marched among the National Front Youth movement.
Le Pen later said the "Nazis" in the crowd had been National Front opponents attempting to embarrass his party in front of the television cameras.

At the labour rally, the three biggest unions -- the pro-Socialist CFDT, the CGT, and the non-partisan Force Ouvriere (FO) -- demonstrated together for the first time in 14 years with two main teaching unions, the FSU and the FEN.
But both the CFDT and FO union leaders stayed away, highlighting personal and policy differences over cuts in working hours and other jobs and welfare issues.
